title: Bernoulli Flow Lab
description: A visual-first investigation of how pipe area, average velocity, pressure, and elevation terms relate in an ideal horizontal two-section flow model.
learningOutcomes: Predict how reducing a circular pipe section changes average velocity at fixed volumetric flow rate.
Relate pressure, average velocity, and elevation terms using the ideal two-point Bernoulli equation.
Read pressure and velocity measurements at two linked points in a horizontal contraction.
State why the ideal model does not represent real losses, cavitation, transients, or equipment ratings.

blocks.text: Two linked measurement points show the same volumetric flow rate while area, average velocity, and ideal pressure redistribute across the contraction.
Continuity connects area and average velocity. Bernoulli's equation then connects pressure, velocity, and elevation for the stated ideal conditions. Detailed derivation is optional in Deep Dive.

blocks.name: Two-point Bernoulli equation
blocks.expression: P1 + rho v1^2/2 + rho g z1 = P2 + rho v2^2/2 + rho g z2

Complete five concise questions after the visual experience. This pilot does not add a new graded assessment.

At fixed incompressible flow rate, a smaller area produces greater average velocity. In the ideal horizontal Bernoulli model, that velocity increase is accompanied by lower static pressure while total ideal head is conserved.

blocks.note: Supports volumetric flow rate, continuity, Bernoulli terms, and the ideal pressure-velocity relationship.

blocks.title: Area redistributes velocity and pressure
blocks.description: A concise explanation connects continuity to Bernoulli without preceding the interaction.
blocks.principle: For steady incompressible flow, the same volumetric flow rate passes both sections. A smaller area therefore increases average velocity; under this horizontal frictionless model, static pressure decreases as velocity increases.
blocks.expandedExplanation: Continuity gives the section velocities. The ideal Bernoulli equation then balances pressure, velocity, and elevation terms between the selected points.
blocks.safetyInformation: The relationship does not include losses, cavitation, transients, or equipment ratings.

blocks.prompt: At fixed incompressible flow rate, what happens to average velocity when circular area decreases?
blocks.answerExplanation: From Q = A v, the same flow rate through a smaller area requires greater average velocity.

blocks.prompt: For the horizontal frictionless pilot, which change accompanies greater section 2 velocity?
blocks.answerExplanation: With equal elevation and no loss or machine-work term, the pressure term decreases as the velocity term increases.

blocks.prompt: Which is the internal SI unit for volumetric flow rate?
blocks.answerExplanation: Display flow in L/s is explicitly converted to m^3/s before engineering calculation.

blocks.prompt: Which ideal head term is zero at both points in this pilot?

options.text: Elevation head relative to the selected datum.
Pressure head for positive absolute pressure.

blocks.answerExplanation: The pilot is horizontal and defines z1 = z2 = 0 m relative to its selected datum.

blocks.prompt: Why is this ideal result insufficient for professional pipe-system design?

options.text: It omits real losses, transients, cavitation, equipment ratings, and design constraints.

blocks.answerExplanation: The pilot is intentionally restricted to the declared ideal assumptions and educational ranges.

blocks.title: Energy terms, SI units, and model limits
blocks.description: Optional detail preserves the full equation, head form, assumptions, and exclusions.
blocks.content: Continuity first determines section-average velocities from the same volumetric flow rate. Bernoulli's equation then balances pressure, kinetic, and elevation terms between points. Dividing the pressure form by rho g expresses pressure head, velocity head, and elevation head in metres. This pilot fixes equal elevation and excludes viscosity, roughness, fittings, turbulence, compressibility, pump or turbine work, heat transfer, transient flow, cavitation, and equipment ratings.
